$comment: CDOCTDR seed registry: draft canonical IDs for the 38 Doctors of the Church. Original compilation in the registry's own words; Latin name-forms follow the Roman Martyrology (CRMEDR) and the papal declaration decrees. All IDs and fields are drafts pending CETF review (docs/schema-proposal.md).
id_scheme: doct:<latin-lemma> (Latin nominative lemma, aligned with CRMEDR)

sources.note: Background reading only; no third-party table is captured. The declaration decrees are the authority for Latin name-forms, popes, years, and honorifics.

entries.name: Ambrose
entries.significance: Bishop of Milan who confronted imperial power, catechized and baptized Augustine, and shaped Latin hymnody; one of the four great Latin Doctors named together by Boniface VIII in 1298.

entries.name: Jerome
entries.significance: Ascetic scholar whose Latin translation of the Bible (the Vulgate) and voluminous biblical commentary made him the foremost textual authority of the Western Church.
entries.note: Stridon's exact site was destroyed in antiquity and its location is disputed by historians; conventionally placed near the modern Croatia–Slovenia border.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.significance: Bishop of Hippo whose Confessions and City of God, and whose theology of grace, sin, and predestination, became the single most influential body of thought in Western Christianity.

entries.name: Gregory the Great
entries.significance: Pope (590–604) who reformed the liturgy and Roman clergy, sent missionaries to evangelize the Anglo-Saxons, and left a body of pastoral and exegetical writing foundational for the medieval Church.
entries.note: Death year 604 places century at 7 by the death-year formula, though Gregory is conventionally regarded as a 6th-century figure (pope 590–604).

entries.name: Thomas Aquinas
entries.significance: The pre-eminent scholastic theologian; his synthesis of faith and reason in the Summa Theologiae shaped Catholic theology and was commended by Leo XIII as a model for study.

entries.name: Athanasius
entries.significance: Bishop of Alexandria and tireless defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism through repeated exiles; his Life of Antony helped spread the monastic ideal.

entries.name: Basil the Great
entries.significance: Bishop of Caesarea and organizer of Eastern monasticism whose ascetic rule and social charity, together with his defense of the Trinity, mark him as a leading Cappadocian Father.
entries.note: Shares one joint 2 January eulogy with Gregory of Nazianzus in the Roman Martyrology (mr:0102).

entries.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
entries.significance: Briefly patriarch of Constantinople, whose orations on the Trinity earned him the title 'the Theologian' among the Cappadocian Fathers.
entries.note: Shares one joint 2 January eulogy with Basil the Great in the Roman Martyrology (mr:0102).

entries.name: John Chrysostom
entries.significance: Patriarch of Constantinople renowned for his eloquent biblical preaching (earning the epithet 'Golden-Mouthed') and his reforming criticism of clerical and imperial excess, which led to his exile and death.
entries.note: mr_ref corrected: the spec's working mr:0913-ioannes-chrysostomus does not exist in CRMEDR; the actual entry is mr:0914-ioannes-chrysostomi (14 September, genitive form). Death year 407 places century at 5 by the death-year formula, though Chrysostom's career is centered in the late 4th century.

entries.name: Bonaventure
entries.significance: Franciscan Minister General and mystical theologian whose Itinerarium Mentis in Deum fused Augustinian and Franciscan spirituality; also an early biographer of St. Francis of Assisi.

entries.name: Anselm of Canterbury
entries.significance: Archbishop of Canterbury and 'father of Scholasticism' whose Proslogion advanced the ontological argument for God's existence and whose Cur Deus Homo shaped Western atonement theology.
entries.note: Death year 1109 places century at 12 by the death-year formula, though Anselm's major philosophical work belongs to the 11th century.

entries.name: Isidore of Seville
entries.significance: Archbishop of Seville whose encyclopedic Etymologiae preserved and transmitted classical learning through the Visigothic kingdom into the medieval West.
entries.note: Exact birthplace is disputed by historians; also given as Cartagena.

entries.name: Peter Chrysologus
entries.significance: Archbishop of Ravenna celebrated for concise, vivid homilies that earned him the epithet 'Chrysologus' (golden-worded), a pastoral counterpart to Chrysostom in the Latin West.

entries.name: Leo the Great
entries.significance: Pope (440–461) whose Tome shaped the Christological definition of Chalcedon and who famously persuaded Attila the Hun to turn back from Rome.
entries.note: mr_ref points to CRMEDR's papal-frame entry for Leo I (mr:1110-leo-i) rather than a doctor-specific entry, reflecting the Roman Martyrology's convention of commemorating him under his papal reign.

entries.name: Peter Damian
entries.significance: Monastic reformer and cardinal whose Liber Gomorrhianus attacked clerical corruption and who was a driving intellectual force behind the eleventh-century Gregorian Reform.

entries.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
entries.significance: Cistercian abbot whose preaching drove the order's rapid expansion and the Second Crusade, and whose sermons on the Song of Songs are a classic of Christian mystical theology.

entries.name: Hilary of Poitiers
entries.significance: Bishop of Poitiers and the foremost Western opponent of Arianism in his day, whose De Trinitate laid Latin foundations for later Trinitarian doctrine.

entries.name: Alphonsus Liguori
entries.significance: Founder of the Redemptorists and moral theologian whose Theologia Moralis, tempering rigorism with pastoral compassion, became a standard reference for confessors.

entries.name: Francis de Sales
entries.significance: Bishop of Geneva whose Introduction to the Devout Life popularized a gentle, accessible spirituality for lay Christians during the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

entries.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
entries.significance: Bishop of Jerusalem whose Catechetical Lectures to candidates for baptism remain a primary witness to fourth-century sacramental instruction.
entries.note: Birthplace Jerusalem; birth_country left null given contested sovereignty, following the CRPDR precedent.

entries.name: Cyril of Alexandria
entries.significance: Patriarch of Alexandria and chief architect of the Christological victory at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius, securing the title Theotokos for Mary.

entries.name: John Damascene
entries.significance: The last of the great Greek Fathers, whose Fount of Knowledge systematized Eastern theology and whose writings defended the veneration of icons during the iconoclast controversy.

entries.name: Bede the Venerable
entries.significance: Northumbrian monk of Jarrow whose Ecclesiastical History of the English People earned him the title 'Father of English History,' alongside pioneering work on chronology and the calendar.

entries.name: Ephrem the Syrian
entries.significance: Syriac deacon and hymnographer, called the 'Harp of the Holy Spirit,' whose vast body of liturgical poetry defended orthodoxy against Arianism and Gnosticism in the Christian East.

entries.name: Peter Canisius
entries.significance: Jesuit theologian whose widely used Catechisms were a central instrument of Catholic renewal in the German-speaking lands during the Counter-Reformation.

entries.name: John of the Cross
entries.significance: Co-founder, with Teresa of Ávila, of the Discalced Carmelite reform, and author of the Dark Night of the Soul and Ascent of Mount Carmel, classics of Christian mystical poetry.

entries.name: Albert the Great
entries.significance: Dominican polymath and teacher of Thomas Aquinas whose integration of Aristotelian natural science with theology made him a pioneer of the medieval university curriculum.

entries.name: Robert Bellarmine
entries.significance: Jesuit cardinal and leading Counter-Reformation controversialist whose Disputationes systematically defended Catholic doctrine against the Reformers; later a central figure in the Galileo affair.
entries.note: mr_ref uses CRMEDR's Italianate spelling 'Bellarmino' rather than the Latinate 'Bellarminus' used in the doct: slug.

entries.name: Anthony of Padua
entries.significance: Franciscan friar renowned for his powerful preaching and command of Scripture, and one of the most widely venerated saints for popular devotion.

entries.name: Lawrence of Brindisi
entries.significance: Capuchin friar and linguist who served as papal diplomat and preacher across Europe, and who accompanied imperial forces against Ottoman armies in Hungary.

entries.name: Catherine of Siena
entries.significance: Dominican tertiary and mystic whose forceful letters and personal intervention helped persuade the papacy to return from Avignon to Rome; author of the Dialogue.

entries.name: Teresa of Ávila
entries.significance: Carmelite reformer and mystical writer whose Interior Castle and Life describe the soul's ascent to union with God; foundress of the Discalced Carmelite reform.

entries.name: Thérèse of Lisieux
entries.significance: Carmelite nun whose autobiography Story of a Soul articulated the 'Little Way' of spiritual childhood; the youngest person ever named a Doctor of the Church.

entries.name: Hildegard of Bingen
entries.significance: Benedictine abbess, visionary, and composer whose writings ranged across theology, medicine, and natural science, making her one of the great polymaths of the twelfth century.

entries.name: John of Ávila
entries.significance: Priest and spiritual director known as the 'Apostle of Andalusia,' whose preaching and mentorship shaped a generation of Spanish Counter-Reformation reformers, including Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross.
entries.note: mr_ref uses CRMEDR's spelling 'de Abula' rather than 'de Ávila' used in the doct: slug.

entries.name: Gregory of Narek
entries.significance: Armenian monk and mystic poet whose Book of Lamentations is a foundational work of Armenian spiritual literature, revered as a national and spiritual father of Armenian Christianity.
entries.note: Narek (near Lake Van, modern Turkey) lay in historic Armenian Vaspurakan. mr_ref is null: Gregory is not commemorated in the Roman Martyrology's 2004 editio typica altera. Death year 1003 places century at 11 by the death-year formula, though he is conventionally described as a 10th-century figure.

entries.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
entries.significance: Bishop of Lyon whose Adversus Haereses was the definitive refutation of Gnosticism and whose formation in the Greek East and ministry in the Latin West made him a bridge figure between the two halves of the early Church.
entries.note: Birth and death years are approximate, per patristic convention for the 2nd century. Death year 202 places century at 3 by the death-year formula, though Irenaeus is conventionally a 2nd-century figure. Tradition defaulted to 'greek' (language and patristic lineage) though he served as bishop of Lyon in the Latin West — see design spec open question 3.

entries.name: John Henry Newman
entries.significance: Convert from Anglicanism, cardinal, and theologian of conscience, doctrinal development, and the harmony of faith and reason; proclaimed a Doctor of the Church on All Saints' Day 2025.
entries.note: Canonized 2019, after the editio typica altera (2004); absent from CRMEDR, so mr_ref is null pending a future edition.
